item.title: Autism Neurodivergence and High-Control Churches
item.description:
Autism

Autism Neurodivergence and High-Control Churches

Autism may draw people to high-control churches, with struggles after arrival.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Extreme structure and prescribed peer groups can attract people with autism to high-control churches.
  • Once there, many report mental exhaustion, excess shame, and feeling overwhelmed by imposed social activities.
  • More thorough research is needed to understand risk.

This post was authored with input from my wife, Kari Puchovich.

High-control churches receive a lot of attention these days. Not so much from the mainstream news media, although there are exceptions. Instead, public interest is expressed in the popularity of documentaries and top-selling books—something Forbes calls “the cult content boom.” Amazon, HBO, Hulu, Max, Netflix, and Paramount are all in the game.

What Is a High-Control Church?

Many people equate high-control churches with cults, but the former term is newer, having emerged from the sociological and religious studies literatures in part because the word cult can be offensive. In the press, cults are often linked to tragic outcomes, such as those suffered at Jonestown, and by the Branch Davidians and Heaven’s Gate.

High-control churches, by contrast, encompass a much broader swath of religious organizations found in many of our communities. The University of Southern California Office of Religious and Spiritual Life lists a number of characteristics of high-pressure religious groups, a concept synonymous with high-control churches. These characteristics include:

  • exclusive beliefs—a singular understanding of God and the road to salvation
  • authoritarian leadership—an unfailing, usually charismatic leader who cannot be questioned without punishment
  • isolation and alienation—new friends are chosen for members while ties with old friends are severed
  • high commitment and exploitation—most of members’ time and much of their money go to the church
  • fear tactics—threats of retribution from God for those who leave the church
  • manipulative recruitment—new members are often recruited through deceptive means
  • pressure and deception—friendship, gifts, and emotional support are given out of apparent kindness ("love bombing"), but with undisclosed expectations of exclusivity
  • totalitarian worldview—critical thinking and higher education are discouraged
  • restrictive behavior—acceptance within the church is contingent on strict guidelines for behavior, including attire, romantic involvements, and friendships

Before meeting my wife, Kari, 11 years ago, I knew nothing about high-control churches. The brand of Catholicism I was raised in revered education, encouraged associations with people inside and outside the church, and respected others’ religious beliefs. Sure, there was pressure to conform, but the church was nothing like the bullet points listed above.

article continues after advertisement

A couple of years before we met, Kari left a church she’d attended for over a decade—one that met all of the criteria the USC Office of Religious and Spiritual Life lists. The experiences Kari described when leaving the church sounded to me, a clinical psychologist, like escaping an emotionally abusive, controlling relationship, something others have also described.

Over many months, Kari was reeled back into the church repeatedly through shaming and fear tactics, before she finally broke away. Having developed a local reputation for outspokenness about her decision to leave, Kari now helps others who are unhappy with the church do the same.

Meeting Former Church Members

I’ve never met an active member of Kari’s former church. Active members have been discouraged from talking with her since she shared her experiences on local media a few years ago. In the past decade, however, I’ve met many former church members, their partners, and some of their children.

Very early on in these meetings, I sensed a pattern of discomfort and disconnection during our social interactions. Not from everyone, but from enough people that it seemed unusual. I chalked it up to the situation, with me as an outsider among people who’d been taught to distrust outsiders. These kinds of messages take time to undo.

article continues after advertisement

Somewhat later, I learned that one of Kari’s former church-going friends was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, which he was forthcoming about during our one-on-one conversations. Given my clinical training and former affiliations with two university centers specializing in neurodivergence, I had a hunch well before he told me, but I thought little of it. Many of us are neurodivergent in one way or another.

Autism Neurodivergence and High-Control Churches

Within a year I learned of another former church member who was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, and within five years I learned of several more. Most were diagnosed after leaving the church, and several of their children are affected. These numbers didn’t make sense to me, even though the sample was quite small.

I turned to the psychology and theology literatures to identify any known links between high-control churches and autism neurodivergence. Scientific studies are scant, and most theoretical papers address the experiences of people with autism in Christianity more broadly.

Authors with positive views of religious and high-control church involvement for people with autism note that both meet needs for structure, sameness, and well-defined, even distanced rules for romantic involvements. Such views are quite common online.

By contrast, research with those with lived experience reveals high rates of sensory and physical exhaustion, feelings of being overwhelmed with required social activities, and a greater sense of shame about personal "failings" and violations of church rules. Others describe an "allure" of high-control churches for young people with autism, and vulnerability to sexual exploitation.

Some academic theologians have called for safeguards to protect neurodivergent people from “spiritual abuse,” defined by absolute authority, excessive restrictions on behavior, demands for blind obedience, and discouraging critical thinking—key items from the bulleted list above.

Views of Former Church Members

Given such limited research, Kari polled members of her Facebook group, comprised of former church members, to ask them openly about their experiences. Some reported being diagnosed after leaving the church. Others mentioned autism-related burnout, rigid aspirations of spiritual perfection, and crushing disappointment of letting God and others down.

article continues after advertisement

There was talk of fatigue from unending social commitments and ambivalence over leaving versus staying in an environment that taxes social capacities while providing well-defined structure for behavior. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) neurodivergence came up as well.

All of this verifies the descriptive research summarized above, and once again, the number of people with autism neurodivergence who responded was large given the overall group size.

The take-home from all of this seems straightforward. We need more research on the appeal and effects of high-control churches on people with autism neurodivergence and on how to protect them from potential harm. Google Scholar returns 1.57 million hits for published studies on autism spectrum disorder since 1995, yet only a handful address the effects of high-control churches.

item.title: What Flight Delays Teach Us About Emotional Regulation
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

What Flight Delays Teach Us About Emotional Regulation

Composure under stress is a buildable skill for companies and individuals.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Losing composure in public has social cost that is greater for some than others.
  • The regulation many women bring to teams is a trained skill that is expected without recognition or credit.
  • Rewarding the loudest person in the room mistakes emotion dysregulation for authority.

This week, I got stuck in the middle of grounded and delayed flights at airports across the country. I jokingly texted my husband, "I swear flying right now is like: here's a tightrope, tie it between these two buildings and get across. Also, the rope is old, and we don't know where to tie one end of it yet."

We were both traveling from the same conference, at different times, into a wave of airport delays that hit thousands of travelers all over the U.S. Tensions were high—and that's exactly when you often get to see the best and worst in people, because stress reveals how leaders, at every level, guide a room through uncertainty.

On the first day of my two-day attempt to get home, a man near me lost it after a delay announcement. He shouted he was “never” flying this airline again. “No one” does their job. “Everyone” around him was an “idiot.” When the flight was ultimately canceled, he slammed his bag on the floor and started calling one person after another, repeating the same complaints, seemingly seeking help regulating himself in the only way he knew how: by shouting his anger out for someone else to catch.

Within minutes, another man appeared to catch the contagious emotion. At the counter, he shouted at the gate agent: “Do your job! Tell us what’s going on!” She quietly responded that there was no new information yet. He didn't believe her. He ranted that everyone deserved to know “right now!”

She eventually left her station and sat down. She still didn't have any answers; she just needed to rest. At this point, a third man stepped in and gently told the second one, "We're all in this together trying to manage it. We need to take a breath."

It seemed to work. The emotion contagion stopped spreading.

Meanwhile, nearly every woman around me in that crowded gate was calmly gathering information, comparing notes, planning next steps. I said as much to one of them. She laughed. "Yeah. That guy would have totally been my husband if he was here with me." Other women joined in, some of them stranded since the night before, all of them frustrated, none of them contaminating anyone with it.

The Privilege Behind Expressed Anger and Entitlement

The two men who loudly expressed their anger and expectation of service that day could do something most women in that gate couldn't (or didn’t): throw a public fit without fearing real consequences. They could command a room's attention until they were finished.

That's a form of power. It's also rarely recognized as one. There is a social cost for women and marginalized people who express anger and entitlement the way those men did: They would likely be labeled difficult, emotional, unprofessional, unhinged, and often many much worse derogatory insults and slurs. Holding back is a survival mechanism.

What Gets Called Leadership, and What Doesn't

The emotion regulation those women showed likely wasn't just a personality trait. Sure, for some it could be—but many women, regardless of personality, learn from a young age to absorb the tension at work and at home.

This skill isn't itself gendered. It's a skill that anyone can learn. But it’s invisible—so when it works, you don’t know it. You only notice it when it’s not there. And it can look effortless, even though it takes constant vigilance.

article continues after advertisement

The third man who stepped in to calm the second man down became a small, visible hero of the gate. The women doing the same work all around him, all day, received no such admiration, nor were they seen as leaders.

Meanwhile, the loudest, most dysregulated people often get the most attention. People rush to comfort them instead of rewarding the ones who demonstrated real patience and self-restraint without drawing attention to themselves.

5 Stress Responses and Their Costs

I went back to the airport the next day. Despite similar delays, there was a felt difference. The gate agents gave consistent updates, even when minor: "We heard they just arrived." "They’re pulling up." When the new crew finally showed up, a woman jumped up and rallied the whole gate to cheer them on. As the crew walked through, the pilot grinned and said, "Sorry we're late, we got stuck in a phone booth changing." We laughed. We stayed calm despite additional delays.

The difference was based on both stress responses and communication. From and individual stress response, I saw five across two days:

  1. Contagious extreme language and negative emotions. A short fuse and all-or-nothing language (never, no one, everyone), like the first man. On a team, it spreads.
  2. Entitlement. Expecting immediate responsiveness or answers that aren’t yet available. It teaches the people around you to scramble, or to lie. It erodes trust.
  3. Active calming. Stepping in to help someone else regulate. This strengthens leadership in the moment, though is carries a cost: absorbing other people's stress without limits can burn out the person doing it.
  4. Comic relief. Easing tension with humor, the way that pilot did. It's a uniquely underrated form of leadership, but hard to do well.
  5. Shutting down. Going quiet and sitting out when it becomes too much. It's understandable when you're asked to respond with no support, but it limits problem-solving.

What Leaders and Organizations Can Do

  1. Recognize and appreciate when a woman regulates a room, not just when a man does it once. Notice especially if the people holding the teams together are never credited for providing that additional emotional labor.
  2. Stop rewarding loudness as a proxy for authority. The loudest person is often the least regulated one, not the most capable. Promotion patterns that consistently reward loudness instead of emotional capacity signal an unhealthy work culture.
  3. Equip frontline customer-facing employees, disproportionately women and marginalized people, with real information. Withholding information asks the people with fewer resources and power to absorb disproportionately greater interpersonal stress.
  4. Build emotion regulation as a trainable, critical, required skill for everyone. The skill some people already have was practiced and earned, often at a cost. Teach it deliberately instead of continuing to rely on the people who already carry it.
